title: The Summit of Life
intro: Husam al-Dosari pictures middle age as a mountain summit from which he can see his youth behind him and the end of life ahead. He borrows the hearthstones and abandoned dwellings of classical Arabic poetry to look for the place where his youth once lived. Even an empty campsite has more to show for itself. From that discovery comes an older brother’s counsel about friendship, time, and the changeable heart that must decide what to do with both.

translation: Here you are at the summit of life, my man.
Are you pleased to be here, or has fear overtaken you?
1.sharh: The speaker meets himself at the highest point of his life. Reaching a summit normally calls for pleasure, but from here he can see the descent ahead.

translation: Time has driven you hard towards its peak.
Youth was barely complete before it rose to leave.
2.sharh: Time drives him as one might drive an animal uphill. Youth, meanwhile, has an independent will and gets up to leave just as it reaches its fullness.

translation: Today you are like a man kneeling on a mountain,
awed by the horizon the mountain had kept from view.
3.sharh: The climb has changed what the man can see. The mountain that once blocked his view now gives him a vantage point so wide that he sinks to his knees.

translation: Behind me lies a youth that has gone for ever.
Grey hair and my appointed end now come towards me.
4.sharh: The voice turns from “you” to “me”. Past and future become directions in space, and the things ahead of him are themselves moving towards him.

translation: Youth has gone. Would you seek it after parting?
Far, far away. Earlier generations never won it back.
5.sharh: He catches himself looking for youth as one might look for an absent friend. The repeated cry of distance carries the experience of all who tried before him.

translation: Can you see hearthstones where it used to spend the spring,
or a campsite whose curve of sand might waken hope?
6.sharh: At an abandoned camp three stones would once have supported a cooking pot. Even one such recognisable mark would give him somewhere to begin looking for his youth.

translation: Those who break camp leave ruins that eyes can still see.
Of youth there is neither trace nor ruin.
7.sharh: The old poems let the returning lover revisit the ground on which the tents once stood. The speaker has lost something that never occupied a piece of ground to begin with.

translation: What road can lead to reunion when the dwellings have vanished
and the roads have taken you so far away?
8.sharh: Two separate losses make a reunion impossible. The place can no longer be recognised and the traveller himself has been carried a long way from it.

translation: When it turns cold, turn away from that old intimacy.
Once you dye your hair, can you still hope for those friendships?
9.sharh: He treats youth as a friend who has withdrawn its affection. Hair dye might restore the colour visible in a mirror, but cannot bring back the company he used to keep.

translation: Marvel at grey age, feeding on a body,
while meeting it brings life to a soul that feeds on deeds.
10.sharh: Grey age seems to feed on bodily strength. The same encounter can quicken a soul whose nourishment is the good it still has time to do.

translation: Body and soul are like opposites under one roof.
When this one settles in, the other moves away.
11.sharh: The two inhabitants share a dwelling but seem to take turns occupying it. The speaker is trying to account for his own experience of insight growing as bodily strength ebbs.

translation: You scarcely see them come even. Whenever
one bends out of shape, the other straightens.
12.sharh: A bent line alongside a straight one makes the imbalance visible. What feels like loss in one part of a person may coincide with a gain in another.

translation: Do you grieve today because a lifetime hurried past?
All creatures have lives that hurry by.
13.sharh: The man’s grief comes from feeling that his own years went exceptionally fast. The echo of “hurry” in both halves brings his experience back within the common lot.

translation: Little brother, listen to counsel from a man
of middle years, dismounted from the youth you too must leave.
14.sharh: The affectionate diminutive makes the teacher an older brother. He speaks as a rider just dismounted from the stretch of road his younger companion is still travelling.

translation: Not long ago he stumbled in his youth.
Only lately he reached a lookout above great ordeals.
15.sharh: His authority comes with a confession of recent error. The high lookout returns us to the opening mountain, now with the difficulties of the ascent still fresh in mind.

translation: Look closely today at that grey-haired woman of false affection.
She has turned aside while you busy yourself courting her.
16.sharh: The ageing woman personifies worldly life. The sharpest detail is the timing of the two actions, her turning away and his still trying to win her.

translation: Perhaps when your soul comes round from its drunkenness
it will stand and speak like a greenhorn making it up,
17.sharh: Attachment to the world has kept the soul intoxicated. On coming to itself it can offer only the unrehearsed explanation that follows in the next verse.

translation: “Did my folly drag me here when hope deceived me?
I have neither she-camel nor camel in this affair.”
18.sharh: The soul realises too late that it had no stake in the affair. Al-Maydani records the entire second half in a verse by al-Ra'i. The speaker owns neither of the camels over which others might quarrel.

translation: Your self-deception is only an ember kindled
for a night. Come morning the flames are put out.
19.sharh: Self-deception has the brightness of a fire in darkness. The speaker measures its entire promise by the few hours between lighting up and morning.

translation: Settle the matter firmly and give up disputing,
little brother. What good will the argument do?
20.sharh: The older voice returns to the practical moment of decision. Continuing the argument consumes the very time about whose passing the two have been speaking.

translation: Take resolve along on any road you follow, and go on.
Those who travelled with true resolve have arrived.
21.sharh: The traveller who could find no route back to youth is given a road forward. Resolve accompanies him for the whole journey, beyond the instant of setting out.

translation: Befriend the noble man and seek no one in his place.
Quick to help in ease, he is brave in hardship.
22.sharh: His idea of a noble friend has two tests. In easy times he responds promptly to another’s need, and in straitened times he still has courage to give.

translation: Beware the base man risen high who hides his faults.
Go right when his path veers left.
23.sharh: High standing can hide a person’s faults from someone choosing a friend. He urges his listener to keep enough independence to go the other way.

translation: Beware humiliation and weak surrender.
Even the dung beetle, given speech, would cry, “Beware.”
24.sharh: The tiny creature in the dirt is given the same warning cry as the man on the summit. Its unlikely voice makes the demand for self-respect hard to forget.

translation: Be sparing with your time. Give no one your share of it.
Show forbearance when people do wrong or act foolishly.
25.sharh: Time is the one possession he is told to guard jealously. In his dealings with the people who make demands on it, he can still afford to be generous in temper.

translation: Make your precious time common property among them
and they will divide up your hidden treasure and squander it.
26.sharh: The treasure can be squandered without a coin visibly changing hands. Each person takes a share of hours whose cost is borne by the owner.

translation: Company, whether with Arabs or with other peoples,
is a draught of medicine whose poison tastes of honey.
27.sharh: The speaker’s distinction concerns the amount of company one keeps, irrespective of who the company is. Honey makes it difficult to tell by taste when one has had enough.

translation: A little does good if you seek health.
Too much is ruinous. Gulping it down is the mistake.
28.sharh: The medicine image turns on how one drinks. A measured draught gives company its value, while gulping it leaves no opportunity to judge when to stop.

translation: What it all comes down to, if you seek its source,
is a turning heart with a natural bent to stray.
29.sharh: The Arabic for “heart”, qalb, shares a root with turning something over. The speaker makes its very name explain why a person’s choices need watching.

translation: Temptations circle it on every side.
Ruses lie in wait around it with every kind of error.
30.sharh: Temptations are first seen circling the heart. The second half makes their movement purposeful, as though someone were finding positions from which to approach it.

translation: The most urgent defence, with a champion hard to find,
guards a morsel of flesh where things mend or fall apart.
31.sharh: The disproportion between the champion and the morsel he guards is deliberate. The wording recalls the prophetic saying that the health of the whole body depends on a small piece of flesh, the heart.

translation: The heart is a fortress. Once its gates are opened,
truth and desires close in and fight.
32.sharh: What enters through the gates will fight for possession of the same small space. Abstract powers become opposing figures crowded together inside the heart.

translation: If it grows pure, you grow pure. Guard what feeds it.
If it harbours sickness, its ills will destroy you both.
33.sharh: The closing “both” joins the owner of the heart to the heart itself. Its gates have become tributaries, and its condition depends on what is allowed to flow into it.

1.1.4.head: سَنام
1.1.4.meaning: The hump of a camel, hence the highest point of anything.

2.2.2.head: وَفى
2.2.2.meaning: To reach completion. This is the sense supplied in the studio caption.

3.2.6.head: زَوى
3.2.6.meaning: To fold or draw together, here to fold the view out of sight.

5.2.6.head: الأُوَل
5.2.6.meaning: Those who came first, the generations that have gone before.

6.1.3.head: أُثفِيَّة
6.1.3.meaning: A hearthstone, one of the stones that supported a cooking pot over the fire.

6.1.6.head: مَربَع
6.1.6.meaning: A spring camping ground or pasture.

6.2.2.head: دِمنَة
6.2.2.meaning: A mark left in the earth by an old encampment.

6.2.4.head: لِوى
6.2.4.meaning: A bend in a stretch of sand.

7.1.3.head: ظَعَنَ
7.1.3.meaning: To strike camp and move on.

7.2.4.head: رَسم
7.2.4.meaning: The faint ground marks of a dwelling that has disappeared.

8.1.6.head: دَرَسَ
8.1.6.meaning: To wear away until little or no trace remains.

8.2.4.head: شَطَّ
8.2.4.meaning: To become distant, to lead far away.

9.2.4.head: خَضب
9.2.4.meaning: Dyeing the hair, often with henna, to cover its greyness.

10.2.4.head: قوت
10.2.4.meaning: The food a living thing depends on, its sustenance.

11.2.2.head: ثَوى
11.2.2.meaning: To settle or stay in one place.

13.2.2.head: بَرِيَّة
13.2.2.meaning: A created being. The plural takes in all living creatures.

14.1.2.head: أُخَيّ
14.1.2.meaning: “Little brother,” an affectionate form of address.

14.2.2.head: تَرَجَّلَ
14.2.2.meaning: To dismount and go on foot.

15.1.3.head: هَفو
15.1.3.meaning: A slip or lapse in judgement.

15.2.3.head: طِلع
15.2.3.meaning: A vantage point overlooking the surrounding ground.

15.2.5.head: جُلّى
15.2.5.meaning: A great ordeal or grave undertaking.

16.1.4.head: شَمطاء
16.1.4.meaning: A woman with grey mingling in her dark hair, here worldly life.

16.1.5.head: ماذِقَة
16.1.5.meaning: Insincere in affection, as milk is diluted by mixing it with water.

17.2.3.head: غِرّ
17.2.3.meaning: An inexperienced person, easily taken in.

18.2.1-7.word: لا ناقَةٌ لِيَ في هَذا وَلا جَمَلُ
18.2.1-7.meaning: “I have neither she-camel nor camel in it” means I have no stake in this affair.

22.2.3.head: نَدب
22.2.3.meaning: Quick to answer a call for help.

23.1.5.head: مَثلَبَة
23.1.5.meaning: A discreditable fault or blemish of character.

23.2.6.head: شِمال
23.2.6.meaning: The left-hand side. Its plural here answers the direction “right” at the beginning of the line.

25.1.1.head: اِضنَن
25.1.1.meaning: Hold a valued possession back, be sparing with it.

26.2.1.head: تَياسَرَ
26.2.1.meaning: To divide something among a group.

27.1.4.head: عُرب
27.1.4.meaning: Arabs, paired here with peoples of other languages.

28.2.4.head: عَبّ
28.2.4.meaning: Gulping down a drink without pausing for breath.

29.2.2.head: قَلوب
29.2.2.meaning: Quick to turn and change, from the same root as “heart”.

31.2.2.head: مُضغَة
31.2.2.meaning: A small piece of flesh, as much as one could chew.

31.2.5.head: رَأب
31.2.5.meaning: Mending a breach, bringing something broken back together.

33.2.2.head: وَعى
33.2.2.meaning: To hold or harbour within oneself.
